x.A: Creating a new AWS Managed Microsoft AD as the identity source means the company would manage users there, but the requirement is to keep managing users and groups in the on-premises Active Directory.
x.B: IAM Identity Center uses AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory with a trust relationship to the on-premises self-managed AD, so users and groups stay managed on premises while getting single sign-on to all accounts.
x.C: A Directory Service trust alone doesn't provide single sign-on across the AWS accounts, because IAM Identity Center isn't enabled.
x.D: An identity provider on EC2 is extra infrastructure to run, and the company wants to keep using its existing Active Directory.

x.A: Aurora Standard charges per I/O request, and with large amounts of traffic the I/O charges grow quickly and aren't predictable.
x.B: Aurora doesn't use a Provisioned IOPS storage type. That's an RDS and EBS concept.
x.C: General Purpose is an RDS storage type, not an Aurora storage configuration.
x.D: Aurora I/O-Optimized has no per-I/O charges and gives better I/O performance for I/O-intensive, high-traffic workloads, so it's the most cost-effective option for heavy I/O.

x.A: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure. It doesn't have compliance standards for NIST and PCI DSS.
x.B: GuardDuty detects threats and doesn't have industry standards for NIST and PCI DSS.
x.C: CloudTrail records API activity and doesn't have security standards to enable for compliance.
x.D: Security Hub supports security standards such as NIST SP 800-53 and PCI DSS, runs automated checks, and aggregates results across accounts through a delegated administrator, so the company can monitor control status and show auditors proof.

x.A: A lifecycle rule to Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on access, so costs fall for rarely accessed objects, and frequently accessed ones stay immediately available. It needs no analysis and has no retrieval fees.
x.B: Glacier has retrieval delays, so it doesn't give immediate availability, and S3 Select doesn't change that.
x.C: Storage class analysis and Standard-IA add manual analysis work, and IA has retrieval fees, which is costly for randomly accessed data.
x.D: Standard-IA plus a Lambda function to move objects back when accessed is custom work and adds retrieval fees.

x.A: Athena SQL JOINs across millions of profiles and connections for five levels is slow and costly, because multiple self-joins are needed.
x.B: Neptune is a graph database built for relationship data, and it finds mutual connections up to several levels efficiently with graph queries over vertices and edges.
x.C: QuickSight visualizes data but doesn't store or query graph relationships efficiently.
x.D: RDS with SQL JOINs for five levels of connections is slow because of the recursive joins across 10 million rows.

x.A: Client VPN is for connecting individual users to a network, not a site connection from the on-premises environment.
x.B: Direct Connect takes weeks to set up and costs much more than needed for low bandwidth and a small amount of traffic.
x.C: A bastion host is for administrative access to instances and isn't a network connection between environments.
x.D: A Site-to-Site VPN is secure, set up in minutes, and the cheapest option for low bandwidth and a small amount of traffic.

x.A: S3 File Gateway provides SMB and NFS file shares, not SFTP, so the company's SFTP authentication and file access mechanisms wouldn't be kept.
x.B: SFTP on EC2 with Auto Scaling means managing servers and AD integration, which is more operational work.
x.C: Transfer Family doesn't support AD Connector as an identity source. It supports AWS Managed Microsoft AD, so connecting through AD Connector doesn't work.
x.D: Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint that stores files in S3, and the AWS Directory Service identity option (AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust to the on-premises AD) lets employees sign in with their AD credentials.

x.A: An SQS queue per step and a transform Lambda function means more components and custom code, and the transformer needs access to all the data.
x.B: SNS message body filtering decides whether a subscriber receives a message, but it doesn't remove parts of the message, so each function would still receive the full order event.
x.C: EventBridge rules with input transformers send only the required fields from the order event to each target Lambda function, and the event bus keeps the components loosely coupled.
x.D: A single transformer Lambda function invoking the validation functions synchronously couples the components tightly and gives the transformer access to all data.

x.A: DynamoDB would require rewriting the application and reports, since the database is MySQL.
x.B: A bigger instance would still run reports and new entries on the same database, so the contention remains.
x.C: Aurora MySQL with multiple read replicas lets the reports run against the reader endpoint, so writes aren't slowed down, and Multi-AZ gives high availability.
x.D: The standby in an Aurora Multi-AZ setup isn't a separate backup instance that you point reports to. Replicas are the readable instances, and they need to be used through the reader endpoint.

x.A: A public virtual interface over Direct Connect reaches S3's public IP addresses without internet access, and it costs the least because there are no extra VPC components or endpoint charges.
x.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic to the internet, which the on-premises network doesn't have, and it adds hourly and data charges.
x.C: An S3 interface endpoint works but has hourly and data processing charges, which makes it costlier than a public VIF.
x.D: VPC peering can't connect an on-premises network to Direct Connect.

x.A: Simple routing returns all values and has no health checks, so it could send traffic to an unhealthy Region.
x.B: Multivalue answer routing returns multiple healthy records and uses health checks, so traffic is distributed across both Regions and an unhealthy Region isn't returned.
x.C: An ALB can't have targets in another Region, so instance IDs from both Regions don't work.
x.D: An ALB in one Region can't use targets from another Region by IP address in a simple way, and it becomes a single point of failure.

x.A: S3 requires employees to use the S3 API or tools instead of a file system, and it doesn't give a mounted file system for the instances in the way the question describes.
x.B: An EBS snapshot mounted as a volume can't be shared across multiple instances in multiple AZs.
x.C: EFS is a shared file system that many EC2 instances across multiple AZs can mount, and it handles large files with no transfers between instances.
x.D: Instance store volumes are local to each instance and are lost if the instance stops, so files can't be shared.

x.A: ACM certificates are for TLS in transit, and can't encrypt a database volume.
x.B: CloudHSM generates keys, but using them to encrypt database volumes needs extra setup and changes, so it's more than the least change.
x.C: SSL encrypts data in transit, not at rest, and KMS keys aren't used for SSL.
x.D: Enabling EBS encryption and RDS encryption with KMS keys encrypts the instance and database volumes at rest, with the fewest changes to the infrastructure.

x.A: A managed NAT gateway scales better, but traffic still goes over the internet, which the company wants to avoid, and it adds data processing costs.
x.B: A larger NAT instance has more bandwidth but still routes S3 traffic through the internet path.
x.C: A gateway endpoint for S3 routes traffic to S3 over the AWS network, bypassing the NAT instance, so the saturated NAT traffic no longer causes timeouts.
x.D: A transit gateway doesn't provide private access to S3, and it adds cost.

x.A: CloudFront is for delivering content to viewers and isn't for accelerating uploads of live streams to the origin over TCP.
x.B: Global Accelerator provides accelerated TCP (and UDP) connections over the AWS global network to the broadcast system, so reporters can send high-quality RTMP streams with low latency.
x.C: Client VPN is for remote access to a network and doesn't accelerate connections.
x.D: EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses don't accelerate connections over long distances.

x.A: Copying EBS snapshots to S3 Glacier Deep Archive isn't a supported direct path, and exporting snapshot data takes effort.
x.B: EBS Snapshots Archive is a lower-cost tier (about 75% less) for snapshots kept long term, and a policy can move the monthly snapshot there for 7 years. It needs little administrative effort.
x.C: Keeping monthly snapshots in the standard tier for 7 years costs much more than the archive tier.
x.D: EBS direct APIs with S3 storage need custom work and aren't a managed approach.

x.A: EFS-to-EFS backup is a solution built on scripts and AWS Backup, not a managed service by itself, and it takes more setup.
x.B: A nightly script to S3 with CRR is custom work and costs more.
x.C: A VPC peering connection with a nightly rsync means managing instances and a script.
x.D: AWS Backup creates a backup plan for EFS that takes daily backups and copies them to another Region. It's a managed service, so it's the lowest effort and cost.

x.A: Read replicas of RDS for SQL Server in both AZs isn't how high availability works, and the web tier is two fixed instances that don't scale.
x.B: A single instance in the Auto Scaling group and a database on two EC2 instances in different Regions is more complex and isn't low effort.
x.C: An Auto Scaling group behind an ALB across two AZs gives a scalable, highly available web tier, and RDS for SQL Server with Multi-AZ is a managed, highly available database with little administration.
x.D: Fixed EC2 instances for the web tier and a self-managed database on EC2 across three AZs means a lot of administration.

x.A: EFS uses NFS, and the application uses SMB, so the application code would need to change.
x.B: FSx for Windows File Server is in AWS, so the on-premises application would see higher latency over the VPN, and it doesn't keep a local copy.
x.C: Snowball is for one-time bulk data transfer and isn't suited to copying hundreds of files every day.
x.D: An AWS Storage Gateway (S3 File Gateway) on premises presents an SMB file share for the application with low latency from the local cache and copies the files to AWS, with no code changes.

x.A: A cron job on an EC2 instance means paying for and managing a server for a task that runs once a day.
x.B: SQS is a queue and doesn't send email messages to employees.
x.C: A scheduled Lambda function scans the table and SNS sends the email. It's serverless, with no servers to manage, and the cost is almost nothing for 15 employees.
x.D: SQS doesn't send emails, so employees wouldn't receive messages.

x.A: A CPU alarm reacts after the load has already increased, so users see the performance impact.
x.B: A recurring scheduled action scales the group up before the holiday peak, so capacity is ready in advance and users aren't affected.
x.C: Raising the minimum and maximum manually during the period is a manual task, and the maximum alone doesn't add capacity.
x.D: SNS alerts on launch events only notify after instances launch and don't add capacity ahead of time.

x.A: Secrets Manager has built-in automatic rotation for RDS for PostgreSQL passwords, so it needs the least work.
x.B: Parameter Store has no native automatic rotation.
x.C: A custom Lambda function to rotate a Parameter Store password means writing and maintaining code.
x.D: KMS key rotation rotates encryption keys, not database passwords, and KMS doesn't store passwords.

x.A: RDS for Oracle doesn't allow privileged OS access that the third-party features need, so replacing them with Lambda would mean extra redevelopment.
x.B: RDS Custom for Oracle gives access to the database environment for the third-party features and supports BYOL, while AWS manages much of the operations, so it's cost-effective.
x.C: DynamoDB can't run Oracle features, and migration would need a complete rewrite.
x.D: PostgreSQL would need the application code to be rewritten, which is costly and slow.

x.A: Third-party software with a tape gateway adds cost and management, and doesn't centralize backups of EC2, RDS, and DynamoDB natively.
x.B: AWS Backup centrally configures, schedules, and monitors backups for EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and other services, replacing the custom scripts.
x.C: Config tracks configuration changes and doesn't take snapshots on a schedule.
x.D: State Manager applies configurations to instances and isn't a centralized backup service.

x.A: RDS with SQL JOINs for many-to-many infrastructure relationships is slow for multi-hop queries, and a relational schema doesn't suit a relationship map.
x.B: Neptune is a managed graph database that fits a map of resources and their relationships. SPARQL (or Gremlin) quickly traverses connections to find risky paths, with little operational work.
x.C: Redshift is a data warehouse, and SQL queries for relationship traversal are slow and not a natural fit.
x.D: DynamoDB with PartiQL isn't suited for traversing relationships across a map of infrastructure.
